utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we've --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. May, excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. We're going to deal, first of all, with legal argument. If you have any other matters, we'll deal with that at the end when we finish this argument. I want to raise something with Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, but it is urgent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the urgent matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Completely personal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked yesterday of you that the programme of work should not be changed because I said that the prison administration authorised a visit for tomorrow afternoon, and you accepted that. You said the schedule wouldn't be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, yesterday, late in the afternoon, the head of the prison informed me that the Dutch Foreign Ministry will not, this time, issue a visa to my wife, which it regularly did beforehand at a written request from your Registry and the Detention Unit's administration. And this time, too, the Detention Unit and the Registry did send in a request in the usual manner on time. They did so well ahead of time. I should like to prevail upon you to intervene to allow me to have this visit, because this is ill-treatment once again, mistreatment of me, because I will be completely isolated. My visits are usually not allowed, and this time my wife's visit has been curtailed. It is the only weekend that has Friday off for her to be able to make that visit. May I also remind you that other prisoners are entitled to visits and have visits for two weeks without any interruption. They have two weekly visits without interruption. The most I have been allowed to have visits for is three days and on one occasion five days, but this time, for completely unknown reasons, this visit has not been approved. I consider this to be part of my physical mistreatment. So please could you prevail and do what you can to make the visit possible? I don't think that the Dutch Ministry has the right to curtail my right to a visit, and I don't think it has anything to do with the affairs conducted here. So could you please do your best to arrange everything with the Detention Unit and everything else, the travelling arrangements and the visa which has this time been -- not been approved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have no powers in relation to this, but we hear what you say, and we will pass on what you've said, and we'll raise it with the Registry now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We wish to call this morning Kevin Curtis. It was the suggestion yesterday by the amici that there are issues arising, I think -- or in fact, it may have been the Court itself that raised them. Can I set out why, in our submission, this evidence ought to be admitted and admitted in full at this stage. The witness is the lead investigator for the Kosovo part of this trial, and the evidence that we seek to lead from him is a general history of the investigation into the trial -- sorry, into the matters subject to the trial, together with an overall analysis and overview of the effect of the evidence so far as the killing sites, as they're described, are concerned. Now, the Chamber indicated yesterday that because there is, of course, hearsay involved in his producing evidence of that kind, that it might not be valuable to the Chamber. Such evidence is, of course, not barred by the Rules of this Tribunal, which doesn't have a rule excluding hearsay, and evidence of, as I am informed and understand, exactly the same general type has been admitted in other cases, or at least certainly in one other case. In Krstic, for example, I believe, the investigator, Ruez, gave evidence along exactly the same lines, summarising the overall effect of what witness statements revealed in circumstances where, as here, the Prosecution adduced live evidence in relation to particular parts of that overall account given by the investigator. So it's not excluded, it always being a matter for the Chamber to decide in due course what weight to attach to any evidence, in particular, of course, to evidence that is categorised in other jurisdictions as hearsay. In our submission, there are two distinct reasons why the evidence should be submitted here, one in a sense procedural and one substantive, and I'll deal with them in order. Looking at the trial overall, from a procedural point of view, as the Chamber knows, it's necessary for us to achieve economies wherever possible because of the scale of the case and because of the inevitable limitations of time. The Chamber knows already that amongst the things we are doing to try to save time is to present, in due course, dossiers of material relating to particular sites. This was partly at the request of the Chamber and has been temporarily halted pending resolution of admissibility issues there, but that's one way we're hoping to achieve economies. And of course, as indicated now for months, I think, our intention overall is to make extensive use of the provisions of 92 bis of our Rules, which allow written statements to go in as evidence, subject to particular safeguards and subject to representations that the accused may make in due course. I'll come back to 92 bis in a minute. These are amongst the things we have to do to try and achieve proper economy. Let me now tell you a little bit about the overall statistics. Over 1.300 statements were taken from witnesses in Kosovo, or in relation to what happened in Kosovo, touching on crime-based matters. Of course, it would be quite impossible for all those witnesses to give live evidence, even if a so-called crime-based witness's evidence only takes one of our one-and-a-half-hour sessions, and that might be optimistic. It wouldn't be possible to have that number of witnesses or anything like it. The Chamber will know that the Prosecution made a selection of events that it could properly hope to deal with in a reasonable period of time, given its duty to prove that events complained of were widespread or systematic. And I think of the 24 sites that one way or another are subject to the indictment, or in respect of those 24 sites, well over 20 statements, on average, witness statements per site have been obtained. The same point arises and has always been in the Prosecution's mind; of course it wouldn't be possible for us to call live evidence from 20 witnesses for that number of sites. These are entirely averaged figures, but it wouldn't be possible if this trial were to be dealt with in a reasonable and timely way. So there has been a reduction of the number of witnesses the Prosecution would seek to present. First it was down to ten per site, and then - and this is just at the time that I became involved in this case - it became reduced further so that in respect of each incident or each site, however we define these matters, there will be something like five witnesses, and the present intention of the Prosecution being to deal with those by one or two live witnesses per site and, again subject to safeguards and representations, the balancing three or four sites being dealt with by adduction through the provisions of Rule 92 bis. We hope, in presenting evidence in that way, that we will be providing sufficient evidence to establish both the substantive crimes and the widespread or systematic basis, but the evidence is necessarily not as complete for any individual sites as it would be if we either had all the ten witnesses or, indeed, I suppose for the events overall, if we had more of those balance of the 1.300 witnesses that we've had to exclude. And thus, for this witness -- or if this witness gives evidence, as the Prosecution would submit would be desirable, then the Chamber will, first of all, have more material to give it a fuller and more comprehensive view of events both individually and collectively. And the Chamber will only have to look at one, probably any one sample of the witness's statement - and I know the Chamber now has the statement before it - to look at one of these accounts - Bela Crkva, for example, on page 6 - to understand how an incident that's described there will necessarily be being described in a -- not an incomplete way but to some degree a necessarily limited way if we only adduce the witnesses that we are currently intending to adduce by way of live witnesses or 92 bis. The evidence would be entirely sufficient, say the Prosecution, but it wouldn't give the Chamber the complete picture that emerges from the officers being able to consider all the other statements. So our first position is that it would be appropriate to take this evidence, to decide in due course the degree to which the evidence should carry weight but to have the evidence now and to have it in mind giving context. And this is very important, and it's important, in our respectful submission, for the Chamber and for the accused to have this evidence before it. First, the Chamber may, in its own judgement and in light of the approach taken by the accused who is now clearly engaging in the trial process - and I'll come back to that in a second as well - the Chamber may, in its own judgement, decide that in respect of particular areas or particular topics, it would wish to have further evidence. The Chamber does not, as I understand it at the moment, have the intention of looking at witness statements itself, and so it cannot know what the balance of available material is. By having this summary of the officer available to it, it can know where there would be more material that it could seek either the Prosecution to call or indeed call itself if it judged that to be desirable or necessary, and so it will be extremely valuable to the Chamber to have this summary before it. I now turn to the accused, who, as I say, is engaging in the trial process, and that is enormously helpful for the trial process and for all of us, but for reasons he's given or for other reasons, he doesn't consider the printed material that's provided to him. The statements reviewed by the investigator Kevin Curtis will have been disclosed to him in one form or another, but it appears he will not have reviewed them himself or apparently have taken the advantage of having them reviewed by anyone else. It's actually very important that the accused should know what the overall material is in order for him to be better informed when it comes to cross-examining or indeed making representations to the Chamber about sufficiency or insufficiency of evidence or making representations about whatever evidence should be called or indeed, in due course, seeking to call evidence from the same collection of evidence himself should that be his choice. And so by having the officer, the investigator, give evidence in this way, which won't take a very great deal of time but which will provide a snapshot of the overall available material, we will be enabling the accused to perform his functions that much the better. Those are really the procedural reasons why -- procedural and associated reasons why, in our respectful submission, this material should be before the Chamber. I then turn to the substantive reason, and it's this: From the accused's opening remarks, it would appear that there may be a head-on challenge to crime-base witnesses if they give evidence in line with what their statements forecast they're going to say. In those circumstances, it may be substantively significant to discover from the officer, from the investigator, that there are signed statements of a consistent kind from the numbers of witnesses of which he can speak. So that there are those two entirely separate reasons why, in our submission, this evidence should be for the Chamber. Can I just turn to two other matters, one I forecast and one I must deal with. 92 bis, just so that we can have a view to where the trial will be going shortly: The Chamber will have seen from the latest version of the witness list that it has had, which I think was dated the 7th of February, and there's an updated version that I'll have made available to all parties as soon as I can, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the 8th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's going to be materially different. And if we look at page 1, we see, in fact, we come to deportations first, which the second proposed witness, Steve Spargo, will deal with, but the overall pattern of evidence is the same. The Chamber will see that, using the projected witness numbers on the left-hand side, numbers 4 and 5 witnesses give evidence of a particular location, and the intention is then to place before the Chamber the 92 bis statements of three further witnesses and then to move on in a live witness, number 6, to the next site, and to follow that with the 92 bis witnesses that relate to that site, and so on. I should say that the list has got slightly out of order so far as connecting 92 bis and live witnesses at the end, but I'll have that corrected in the next day or so. So that's the approach that we were intending to take. That's the approach we were intending to take in order to make matters as comprehensive to Your Honours as could be possible at any given time. And when we come to the sites known as killing sites later on, we'd open that particular passage of evidence with the presentation, if acceptable, of the dossier that would relate to the killing site, seeing how much of that material could go in by way of admission or agreement, and then have the live witness and then follow it with the 92 bis witnesses. So that that's the plan that has been made for the adaption of evidence. The accused has always been on notice by the provision of these witness lists for the last month, in law, of the 92 bis witnesses we intended to adduce. I suspect that he will tell us that he hasn't read those lists and therefore hasn't considered those statements. And it may be convenient, perhaps today, perhaps after one of the adjournments, if we give some thought to the best way of safeguarding his interests so far as this is concerned. One way to deal with it would be as follows: For -- and perhaps with necessary abbreviation of time otherwise provided for in the Rules as may be necessary, to give him notice publicly, before a particular witness is about to be called live, of the written statements that we seek to adduce thereafter under the provisions of 92 bis, possibly summarising very briefly what they will say. Because if he's not alert, or alerted, for whatever reason, to the 92 bis witness statements we seek to adduce, then his cross-examination may suffer as a result, and that would be unfortunate, and we obviously desire to help him. But that's a problem, and I'd perhaps return to it a little later when the Chamber has had an opportunity to think about it. Then the last matter that I must deal with is this: Of the over 1.300 witness statements taken altogether in relation to crime base of Kosovo, a large proportion has been served on the accused in one way or another and on the amici, either as the original confirming materials or since then. The balance of witness statements are being further reviewed for Rule 68 purposes, particularly in light of the accused's indication of his defence from his opening remarks, and in that way we hope to safeguard his interests further, handing over, of course, any statements that appear to be Rule 68 relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me quote you. You mentioned an overall analysis and overview of the effect of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And does it have to be done necessarily in the form of testimony of a witness? I'm asking whether it can be done in the form of opening statements or in pre-trial brief or any brief during the trial. What's the difference between the arguments and evidence? And certainly the witness is entitled to testimony, what he knows, but the latter part of the statement -- I particularly read through the latter part of it. The overall analysis is -- I think it's not a kind -- it's totally hearsay and is of little probative value. What would you make the distinction between the arguments and evidence on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour says that because it's hearsay, it's of little probative value. I would respectfully suggest that in this Tribunal, hearsay material is, of course, of a probative value to be assessed in due course. It may be little, it may be nil, or it may be substantial. But because it's capable of having evidential value, that's a reason for adducing it through a witness rather than simply advancing it in an opening statement or in a written brief, where the material may be said to have no evidential value. So it has to come in as evidence to have some evidential value. As to its evidential value, that will depend on a number of factors, including the degree of cross-examination on it or on associated pieces of evidence by the accused, or indeed by the amici, and will also depend on such matters as the degree of consistency of evidence that may be spoken of if he's cross-examined by the witness, and so on. So that in our submission, of course hearsay, for obvious reasons, and in light of our own sometimes particular backgrounds in systems which exclude hearsay, of course hearsay has to be viewed cautiously. But the appropriate starting point, in our submission, is that it has value and that its value is to be assessed in due course, and that explains why we seek to put it in as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I'd like to suggest is that the overall analysis could be done in the form of brief, and if you are -- in terms of time and efficiency, and if you are arguing that you need some more 92 bis statements or more witnesses, the Court will allow them in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, as to the last point, obviously we are very aware of the timetable that has been set for us and we are by no means confident, particularly in light of cross-examination, that there may not be difficulties in meeting that timetable. And although we would, of course, be optimistic that justified applications for additional witnesses would be met, we have to work on the basis that we may be kept to our present list of witnesses. As to analysis -- and I can simply perhaps take Your Honour back to the example I gave from the witness statement, Bela Crkva. Just simply as an example, and I'm not going to read it out, for obvious reasons, but if the Court is good enough just to read through it and see the sort of details that are covered overall, the number of different issues that are covered, you'll see there's a large range of material covered and simply can't be covered by just one, or even necessarily in this case, the three witnesses currently identified, because it's quite a large story. And you'll see this on, I think, your list. If you have the 8th of February witness list, you'll find it on page 15 of that list, witnesses numbered 50, 51, and 52, with 92 bis witnesses 83, 84, and 85. So this is an exception because of the scale of the event. We've actually proposed to call three witnesses rather than two or one. But even so, the complete story is unlikely to be given by those witnesses, and the overall analysis of which the officer speaks would make for a more complete story, a more complete account, and would enable the Chamber and the accused to know both more about the events and, if there are issues to be joined between the accused and the Prosecution, enable him and the Chamber to know better how to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the issue here is the conclusions of this investigating police officer who has read a large number of statements of witnesses and then presents his own conclusions upon the content of that written material. There's no objection to him giving evidence about the means of investigation and events that he organised or caused to be done as part of the overall investigation so that Your Honours are advised of matters concerning geography, population, and other relevant details. The objection is to him really performing the role which Your Honour has correctly identified was really performed in the opening statement of the Prosecutor where they outlined their allegations against the accused and stated the events that happened that are the subject matter of the indictment. And really, this witness is doing no more, no less than that. He's repeating the allegations of the Prosecutor based on material that's been read by him. And in our judgement, it doesn't advance the issues within the case for the Trial Chamber to properly determine the charges against the accused. It's an analysis of a large number of these sites with reference to events that he was not a witness to, descriptions of men describing killings or other events as being the responsibility of another party, and it's our submission that that fails the test to be properly considered as evidence in a trial. We understand that the Rules are wider within this Tribunal and it is a Tribunal investigating events and matters, as well as a court, and there is not a rule against hearsay, but courts have been cautious about the admission of such evidence because the Judges are aware of the problems that can arise with it. And on the scale of hearsay evidence, this is really the most extreme, where a witness has read the statements of a large number of people, then presents his conclusions to the Court. And really, the responsibility for drawing those conclusions are those of the Judges who are trying the issue, and that is the responsibility of the Judges in this courtroom. So we say that this evidence carries with it great dangers in that form. I don't know if I can assist the Court any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. If you have the statement of Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Chamber's had a chance to look at it. If you look at page 4, there is there a description of the actions of the Prosecution, how they went about their investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't see there can be any objection to that, the means and procedures of the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 4 and on to page 5. And I suppose the description of where a village is, for instance, if that's of assistance, again the witness can give evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Geography and orientation and layout, as well as maps produced. Again, we have no objection. Those are matters that are plainly useful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused would -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. The accused plainly wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're going to exclude this evidence apart from evidence of geography. Is there anything else you want to say to us but on this very narrow point, that's all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to say something with respect to what I heard a moment ago. We are dealing with the suggestion of a complete abuse of the proceedings and prolonging the time for repeating the indictment and the job done by the Prosecution. We have heard the Prosecution. We listened to the Prosecutor and his associates and now we have to go on to listen to the Prosecutor's other staff members, everything within the corps of the Prosecution, all of which should have been contained in the opening statement of the Prosecutor. And in an illegal way, this repetition and the Prosecutor's accusations are being repeated to hurl these untruths and mask the truth. So we're going further and further away now. First of all we had the Prosecutor, then we had his advisors, then we had the clerks and staff, and we'll probably get down to the Prosecutor's driver and hairdresser and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're with you. We're going to exclude it, so there's no need to make the point again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I have another thing to say. I heard a name mentioned, Kevin Curtis. If I understood the name correctly, it was Kevin Curtis. Kevin Curtis is an individual who committed a crime, the crime of my unlawful arrest in Belgrade. He was the perpetrator of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not an appropriate point. We're now going to rule. Mr. Milosevic, be quiet, please. We've considered this evidence. We've had the opportunity of considering it during the adjournment. The reason we're going to exclude it is this: that it is the evidence of an investigator who's read a great many statements and come to various conclusions about them. Those conclusions he wishes to report to the Court. The first objection, of course, is that this is purely hearsay evidence given by a witness who was not present, who didn't hear or see the events which he is going to relate. The fact that it is hearsay does not prevent evidence being given in this Tribunal; we admit hearsay evidence. But on the other hand, we do not admit evidence which is of limited probative value, if any, and in our judgement, to have the conclusions of the investigator relayed to us is of no probative value, as Judge Kwon has already pointed out. In these circumstances, what we would have heard would have in fact been a repetition of the Prosecution case about these various sites. As such, it is of no assistance to us, in our view. We shall hear the evidence of the witnesses. We will hear the submissions of counsel. That will inform us, first of all, of the evidence and of the case. In these circumstances, the evidence will not be admitted. I do point out that there are two of us here today and not three. If the Prosecution want to try to have the evidence admitted with three, they can do so. Now, it's a matter for you, Mr. Nice, whether you want to call the witness on those matters which have been identified in the course of argument, that is, the means of investigation, the geography. Whether it's of any assistance to have that, I don't know. It's a matter for you whether you want to call it or not. We've got maps. No doubt we shall hear about the exhumations in due course when we come to the individual sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My current disposition is probably not to call the officer at this stage, possibly call him later, but I'd like just a moment to discuss that, if I may. I'm certainly not going to seek to overturn your ruling by the presence of His Honour Judge Robinson. It may be that we will return to the issue or some of the issues in due course. I hope not, but it may be, but that's another reason for putting these witnesses back, I think in principle possibly not calling them at all, which will help with the limitation on witnesses to which we are subject in any event. Before I seek just a short adjournment to decide whether to call Mr. Curtis or Mr. Spargo at all, would it be convenient to turn to the 92 bis problem? Because if I don't call either of them, then we'll be directly into the first crime-base witness. If we look at the list again, the list of the 8th of February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you get there, there's Mr. Spargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it not be convenient to deal with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. If different considerations arise, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the different considerations, let me say we've had the statement and we're grateful we have looked at it, and he produces the map. Now, it seems to me the map may well be admissible as a tool, something which can be used during the course of the trial. Clearly the witness can't give evidence about what happened in the various sites, but -- and indeed whether a witness is necessary to produce the map, I don't know. It's something for you to consider. But certainly at first blush, it would appear there may be more merit in that particular argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Well, can we -- can I have a word with Mr. Ryneveld about that? And what I was going to invite the Chamber to consider while I'm doing that is that, one way or another, we're likely to be on to the first crime-base witness, who is here in the building, very soon. If the Chamber looks at the witness list of the 8th of February, there are two witnesses, numbers 4 and 5, and there are then proposed three 92 bis witnesses. As I say, the accused has been on notice for a considerable period of time that the intention is to produce those witnesses by the provisions of 92 bis. A word or so about the process. The Chamber will be aware to some degree of what happens. The 92 bis process happens in the territory, and the formal acknowledging of accuracy of signature is probably done in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful if, since the accused is representing himself, if you briefly introduce the Rule and the procedure so that it may be understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The 92 bis provisions for proof of facts other than by oral evidence, at page 93 of the version of the Rules I have, allows a Chamber to admit "... in whole or part, evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement in lieu of oral testimony which goes to proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment" and sets out a number of factors in favour of admitting the evidence in written form. I should perhaps check whether the accused has been provided with a copy of the Rules. Of course if he hasn't, it would be helpful for him to have one on his bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has a had a copy of the Rules. I will check with the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll provide you with a copy of the Rules so you can have it during the court proceedings if you want to read it and follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation]. Can I say something in response to what the Prosecutor has just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish what he's saying now, and then we'll hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Rules go on to list factors favouring admission of such evidence and factors against it. Rather than list them all, to assist the accused, factors against admission of such evidence include an overriding public interest in evidence being presented orally, an objection by a party demonstrating that the source and nature of the evidence is unreliable or that its prejudicial effect outweighs its probative value or that there are other factors making it appropriate for the proposed 92 bis witness to attend for cross-examination. There are then provisions about declarations that have to be made by the proposed witness, and they've been dealt with on recent missions to the territory, with the assistance of staff of the Registry, as the Chamber may know, and there's a requirement as to what the declaration of the witness has to verify. There are further provisions which needn't concern us, either at all or immediately, about dead witnesses or witnesses who have died. And then it says this, at (E), after dealing with the admission of transcripts of evidence: "Subject to Rule 127 or any order to the contrary, a party seeking to adduce a written statement or transcript shall give fourteen days notice to the opposing party, who may within seven days object. The Trial Chamber shall decide, after hearing the parties, whether to admit the statement or transcript in whole or in part and whether to require the witness to appear for cross-examination." Rule 127 is the Rule, of course, which allows for variation, including abbreviation of time limits. With that brief survey of the Rule and with an eye to the Prosecution's revised amended order of witnesses of the 8th of February, it would be my invitation to the Chamber to ensure by some means that the accused is aware ahead of the calling of the evidence of witnesses 4 and 5. Not only that it is our intention to rely on 92 bis witnesses identified thereafter, but possibly to give him some summary or to give him a further opportunity to read statements from those witness, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't got those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case they must be provided to the Chamber, and that can be done, of course, very swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it may be more convenient to deal with Mr. Spargo now and then to return to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I obviously want the -- I would like the matter to be resolved, if we can, before we call the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Mr. Spargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour has correctly identified the issues which Mr. Ryneveld and I had spoken of in advance anyway. There was a further matter concerning the video material, which we should mention. That's an exhibit within his evidence. There are five videotapes, and we've both agreed that the news reporting - and one is what appears to be private video footage - is admissible as exhibits within the case, but the sound must be off. So if Your Honours look at these videotapes, the sound must be off, because again, rather like the issue with Mr. Curtis, they are the commentary and opinions of journalists and a selection of journalists. But the actual footage itself can be seen. I think Your Honours will know what I'm talking about, because it was all over the world and no passerby could have missed it. But to ensure the integrity of this trial, both parties have agreed that it would be wrong to have such sound on in looking at the videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, what is proposed to be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honour is asking only with respect to the videos or his evidence in chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His evidence generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- I had proposed that this witness really -- I've prepared a summary, which I hope the Court has had an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Oh, my goodness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've seen the statement. We've had that, but not the summary. If we could have the summary now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I have prepared a summary, which includes which exhibits we propose to put in at what time. Basically, there are three categories of evidence that we had proposed. The first category is simply: This witness has produced maps, computer-generated maps, based on the information of the statements by the witnesses, to assist the Court that, when the witnesses testify, that they will be able to see the routes taken by these refugees to the various border points. In other words, for each -- you perhaps saw one of those aggregate maps during the course of the opening. It was a colour map with different coloured routes. That was produced by Mr. Spargo. I do not propose, in light of Your Honour's ruling, to have him expound upon the narrative, unfold the narrative of what witnesses told him. But as a result of that, he created these maps. And for each -- if you can see, perhaps, paragraph 3, I've got the overview map and the proposal for each exhibit. It's the aggregate map of the deportation routes. Then as you get -- for each of the deportation sites only, not the killing sites that I referred to, he will produce some maps that he created, including some town maps, and perhaps we have to have a vehicle by which these can be entered into evidence as proper exhibits. When we then get perhaps to paragraph 11, where I talk about Djakovica, you'll note that there is, under proposed Exhibit K560, a one-and-a-half-hour video depicting destruction to houses, and part of which, a very small part of which, was shown during the opening. I propose to simply enter that video without the necessity of playing it. The Court can -- copies have been given to the amici; the accused has a copy. The Court can -- rather than take up valuable court time, the proposal was simply to mark it as an exhibit and the Court can then view it at a time not during court hours. And as I discussed with Mr. Kay, we agree that, as I did during the opening, no sound. Because it's the footage, it's the visual impressions that are important, not a commentary by a journalist or the person taking it. That was the proposal. Then when we get to paragraph 17, you will note that paragraph 17 is under the heading of "Additional Evidence." In light of the Court's ruling today, I take the view that everything under paragraph 17 would be along the lines of a conclusion drawn by the witness, along the lines that we had originally proposed - it may be of assistance to the Court - by means of Kevin Curtis. I view paragraph 17 to fall within the Court's order, and I would propose not to adduce any of paragraph 17. Finally, at page 5, under tab -- under number 18, I have listed three potential BBC news tapes with various footage of the things depicted in this note, and again, I propose merely to tender the exhibits into evidence without playing them, in the interests of time. And again, all copies have been disclosed to all parties. And should the Court at some point wish to have a witness recalled after viewing the video, the witness is available for re-examination or cross-examination by any of the parties once they've had an opportunity to do so. This is a discretionary matter as to whether or not the Court wants to admit that evidence, but parts of this evidence were shown in the opening. And that is my proposal for Mr. Spargo. I've had discussions with the amici, and as I understand it, they're agreed that paragraph 17 ought not be entered, and they -- and apart from the issue of sound in the videos, I understand there is no objection from the friends of the Court with respect to these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kay, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ryneveld set out the position that we had advanced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, it's proposed now to call Mr. Spargo. You've heard the discussion about him. Is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do wish to say something about that and about what the Prosecutor said earlier on, and I consider that to be my right, the right to react. The Prosecutor said here that I was taking part in the proceedings, which is incorrect. I am not taking part in the proceedings, because I do not recognise the Court. But I did state here publicly that I will use every opportunity to address the public, every opportunity, and I have been given only one in the past seven months, to tell the truth. And what I am saying whenever I am given the opportunity of addressing the public, I think is my duty to have the truth be heard, even opportunities afforded me like the one we saw yesterday here. Secondly, written statements by witnesses completely curtail the right of them being questioned. Every witness has to come here and we must be given a chance of asking those witnesses questions if the witnesses have anything to do with the accusations and indictment against me. I have heard that there are 1.300 written statements. I am then going to hand in to you 130.000 written statements, or 1.300.000 written statements of the victims of crimes that were perpetrated by the terrorists and NATO. I don't think you can abuse the proceedings and trial in this way. Thirdly, relating to the issues as to the crime sites, the so-called crime sites, you are duty-bound to clarify, even in an illegal trial of this nature, that you can speak of a crime site only if you have any evidence and proof that I was present at the site of the crime and that I committed those crimes, or if those crimes actually did take place, and I have my doubts in the majority of cases. So you would have to have proof and evidence that I ordered the perpetrators of those crimes to carry them out; otherwise, what sense and meaning to the spots in which people were killed have to do with the accusations held against me, unless you have prior evidence and proof that this has anything whatsoever to do with me? And it has absolutely nothing to do with me, but it does have something to do with the tactics of the Prosecutor, who wishes, here and now, to swamp and inundate the world public with countless examples of the sufferings of people during a war, without coming to the question, discussing the question of how come the war came about and how come the crimes were committed in Yugoslavia. So you can send this to Clinton, evidence of those crimes, and show him the crimes that were committed, to send them to Clinton and not to me. I had nothing to do with crimes and the crime sites, and all you're doing is swamping the international public with alleged facts. I think this is an essential matter of substance, if you have no proof to show that I was on the spot or that I ordered the perpetrators of the crimes, and you have nothing of the kind. I have presented proof and evidence to the contrary in opposition to all this, that crimes were being in fact prevented, that people were being brought to justice, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is not the time for speeches and submissions except on the narrow issue we're dealing with. As to the relevance of evidence, that's a matter for the Tribunal to rule on, as we will. Very well. Let's call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure where Mr. Spargo is exactly at the moment. I'm pretty sure that I'm not going to seek to put anything in through Mr. Curtis at the moment. I'll tender him in due course if I don't seek to call him for any particular part of his evidence, or possibly if things change, but we'll move straight on to Mr. Spargo. But can we just have a few minutes first to reorganise ourselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn. --- Break taken at 10.34 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Stephen Spargo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should say we'll go on now until 11.15 before we take the longer break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: My full name is Stephen John Spargo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you to keep your voice up, if you would, please. I understand, sir, that you are a police officer and you've been a police officer in Australia since 1977. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You took up your occupation with the ICTY in what year?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: In June of 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were assigned to the Kosovo investigation at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to that, sir, in your capacity as a police officer, did you have any particular training in the capacity as an intelligence analyst?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, in the course of that training, become familiar with the creation of computerised maps?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as part of your overall duties with the ICTY and this investigation, were you tasked at some point with analysing the various statements of individuals from the Kosovo investigation and creating maps with respect to the routes that they allegedly took?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, in a very brief way to assist the Court, indicate how you went about performing that task so that the Court can understand the end product of what you produced.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: The maps were created using a computerised programme called ArcView, which is a geographical information system. It allowed us to electronically plot lines on an electronic map of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the statements that you analysed, sir, I understand that there are some 1.300 some-odd statements in the archives from this particular file. Which statements did you actually use in order to trace these particular routes onto maps? Were they all 1.300 or a restricted portion of them?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: The maps were compiled from the statements which are to be tendered as live witness or 92 bis before the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these maps are based on the witness statements on the witness list tendered by the Prosecution in this case and none other?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I actually get to those particular maps, sir, I understand that there is a Times Atlas map of the Balkans that is available. That may perhaps show the Court perhaps the layout of the Balkans; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Although it's not on the summary sheet, Your Honours - we had intended to introduce this particular map through another witness - but I thought it may be of assistance to the Court if we tender a Times Atlas map of the Balkans. And we have copies here for the Court and for the various parties. Perhaps you could show it to the witness, Mr. Usher. Until we get this process down, the first few exhibits may take a little bit of time. We'll get the process quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have the original here to be marked as the Court exhibit unless -- it should be shown to the witness to make sure that ... Is it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what has been tendered as Exhibit 1, is that a Times Atlas map of the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps you could point out to us where is Kosovo on this map and trace it with a pointer, if you have it.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Kosovo is located here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're now tracing Kosovo on the right-hand bottom of the screen that's on the camera. Ah. Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Albanian border, Macedonian border, the border with Serbia proper, and the Montenegrin border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is then Exhibit 1 in these proceedings, was formerly K5. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us that you were assigned the task of reviewing these statements, and from those statements, sir, without giving us any conclusions, did you in fact create an overview map of the routes described in those statements by the various witnesses by means of which they left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown what we have marked as K6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the ELMO at the moment, Witness, is what is presently marked as K6, and it appears to be a multicoloured diagram. First of all, what is that a map of?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: It is a map of the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And can you tell us, sir, where -- can you point out perhaps where the borders of Kosovo are again on this reduced map?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Of course. The Macedonian border is here, the Albanian border is here, the border with Montenegro, the border with Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record, you've simply outlined with your pointer, starting at the bottom right-hand frame near Macedonia. You've gone in a clockwise fashion around the borders of Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, how did this map come about? Did you create this or how did this come into being?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: The basic map was created using the commercial software of ArcView. On that, I produced the coloured lines of each of the individual indictment sites for the deportation side of the second amended indictment. Each of the colours on the map represents one particular deportation site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps, sir, we can just pick a colour and you could let us know for -- let's start at the very top. The green colour. What do those green lines indicate?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: The green lines here are centred on the deportation site of Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: And show the routes taken by the displaced persons at various times and then on their journey to the border crossings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're now tracing from what on the map -- you called it Vushtrri. Is Vucitrn another way --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Vucitrn is the same place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I see. And it seems to be going to an area marked as Pristina and then down towards what border?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: It goes down through Lipljan, Suva Reka, Prizren, to the border at Qafe e Morina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And let's take another colour. The orange one that seems to have -- around Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Mitrovica shows the routes of displaced persons from the indictment site at Mitrovica through various routes to the border at Qafe e Morina or to the border with Montenegro at Rozaje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm sorry, I skipped ahead. You showed us one of the green routes down to the Albanian border. There also appears to be arrows up towards Serbia to Novi Pazar. What is that -- what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That route is one witness who travelled from the Vucitrn area through Mitrovica, Leposavic to Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, rather than go through each of these colours on this particular map, I understand that you have subsequently generated maps for each of these particular routes in isolation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct. In fact, the starting point was to create a map for each of the individual sites and then to amalgamate them together in one single map, which is this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Rather than go through all of the colours on this particular map, perhaps we could have that now marked as Exhibit 2 in these proceedings. So K6 becomes Exhibit 2; is that correct, Madam Clerk?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just to ensure that the interpreters have an opportunity to interpret my question before you commence your answer, would you please pause. I know it's difficult when we both speak the same language, but there is a pause that needs to be observed for translation.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you create a map for the Orahovac area?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you have produced some 13 maps under collective number K7 for the various deportation sites; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have part of K7 available? I think we have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps during the break, Your Honours, we'll find a more efficient route by which these can be distributed in advance so that we don't have to wait.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir, could you -- I should wait for it to go on the ELMO. For the record, we now have a green colour near the word "Orahovac," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct. That is to define the deportation site, or the municipality in which the deportation took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are a number of communities listed immediately below the word "Orahovac," which is in large letters on the top right-hand corner of the map. What do they signify?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: The names are the villages within that area, some of which were places where persons were deported from; others are mentioned as landmarks in the statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just to be very brief about this, you created this map to reflect what the Court will hear in the statements. As witnesses refer to various towns and places and routes they took, these would then be traced in the green arrows on this particular map. And I believe you've already explained this to us: In the aggregate map, this is how they took the route to the Albanian border; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Exhibit 3, please, Your Honours, part of K7. Since I'm following the summary that the Court has, perhaps I could also now ask for Exhibit K8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that there is a collection of maps, which we have marked tentatively as K8, depicting each municipality as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to this particular community, you've prepared another -- this is a map that you would have prepared on computer?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: These were maps which we obtained from a United Nations body in Kosovo who were responsible for producing maps for the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally do anything to the map or add anything to it or make any markings on it or modify it in any way?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Some of the maps have annotations on them which are relevant to various incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still dealing with the Orahovac municipality, sir, would you look at the ELMO and -- we'll get it on there. There we are. And this is a map that was then provided to you. Did you make any modifications to this particular map?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the legend indicates the village boundaries, the railways, what would be the urban area. That would be in sort of the orange colour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the municipality boundaries and roads are also shown on this map?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct. The thick grey line is the municipality boundary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this map also includes the names of little villages and hamlets within that municipality?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I've lost the number. Are we at 4 now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor Exhibit 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Have copies been distributed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on, then, sir, to the Prizren municipality. First of all, again, the same process was adopted? And I'm not going to do this for each municipality, but again, you analysed the statements, you attempted to draw routes on a map depicting what those statements reflected; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I can then turn to Prizren, part of K7. Is that on the ELMO? So it is. Very briefly, rather than have me do the talking, can you explain what the maps shows.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: The map shows the routes taken by persons from the villages of Pirane, Landovica, and several areas within Prizren itself, and the routes taken to the border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that line where the pink line arrow stops at the bottom left-hand corner, near a body, what is that purple-blue mark? What is that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That area is a body of water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that particular area, is that the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Exhibit 5, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still dealing with Prizren, part of the bundle that we referred to as K8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. You said Exhibit 5? Number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map was submitted together with the other maps under Exhibit 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My proposal -- well, it's up to the Court. If the Court wants to make it a bundle, as it was before, fine, unless we want to give them individual numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it would be more convenient to keep them together, refer to it as Exhibit 2 or 3 and Map 1, 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Fine. Excellent. Thank you. We'll do it that way. I'll let the clerk call the numbers, then, because ... So the map I've just introduced, that is, the map of Prizren that used to be part of K7, is now map what? 2 of Exhibit 3?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 3, map 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving, then, to the bundle K -- I guess now Exhibit 4, used to be K8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is that map on the ELMO? Not yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is map 3 of Exhibit 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, Witness, what is this map?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: This map shows the municipality of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this the map that you received from another UN organisation?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any modifications?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: On this map, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe the clerk has indicated what map this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just for the clarification. That map is part of the Exhibit 4, not number 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That was my understanding as well, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was K --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: K8. It was part of K8 at one time, which I understood became Exhibit 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Staying still with the municipality of Prizren, and tab 24, if Your Honours have tab materials, under what was formerly K24, it's the town map of Prizren. I'm sorry. It was tab 11. It looks like this, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have on the ELMO what I understand is a town map of Prizren. How was this created and by whom?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: This was created by the same body that made the municipality maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does this map depict? I mean, by its name we know it's a town map, but there are arrows on it. How did they get there?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: The arrows were placed on the map to show particular routes around and through the town of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're now referring to the green arrows and you're tracing -- for the record, you're tracing with your pointer from the top left corner of the map down to the -- down the side, and now the right side across to the left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And those are routes within the town of Prizren that are contained in witness statements --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in this case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. May we move on to the village of -- or the municipality of Srbica. This is again part of K7, followed by a map from K8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I'm clear, sir, this is one of the yellow routes that is depicted as well on that aggregate map you earlier introduced; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what does this depict?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: It depicts the routes taken by displaced persons from the vicinity of Izbica to the Albanian border at Qafe e Prushit and to the Albanian border at Qafe e Morina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there are a number of villages marked on the map as well, the smaller villages around Izbica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Clerk, do we have a number for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Map 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Map 4 of Exhibit 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we'll adjourn now. I think at some time we're going to have put these maps in a binder or the like with tab numbers. Otherwise, it's going to be a recipe for confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have that, but I understood that there was -- we'll certainly provide the Court with new binders. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we'll go on with the evidence meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to respond to Your Honour's comment as we broke for the break, I might say that we had originally provided bundles in tabs to all the parties, including to the amici, and a copy was served on the accused. We also, I believe, intended to have these bundles for the Court but that process was arrested when we understood that the Court wanted to have these matters dealt with document by document. So they were deconstructed. We're now in the process of reconstructing them, and they will be given to the Court in the bundle form. We had them that way. But our apologies. Perhaps we misunderstood. So I apologise for the inconvenience for the Court getting these piecemeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's obviously been some confusion and misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And as I say, my friends and the accused do have them in tabbed bundles. Now, I believe if I can turn -- I believe I just finished tab -- or point 6 on the summary, and I'm about to go to the Suva Reka municipality, number 7 on our summary. And I hope to move at a slightly faster pace now that we have the process somewhat down. That would be map number 5 of the -- I'm going to ask the witness to now look at map number 5. That used to be K7. Is that on the ELMO? Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, very briefly, what is this?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: This is a map showing the deportation routes from a number of centres in the Suva Reka municipality. From Belanica in two directions. From Suva Reka and from the village of Lesane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do all of these routes go through Prizren? Am I looking at that correct? In other words, there are two sort of routes forming kind of a circle, joining at Prizren and then going on to the border with Albania?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That was -- I guess that will be map 5, part of Exhibit 3, then. Is that right, Madam Clerk, if I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with that municipality and going to what used to be K8, would you please look at the map that's -- it's Suva Reka municipality. And just very briefly, again we have a legend on the top right-hand corner, indicating roads and railways and boundaries, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make any modifications to this map or is this a map that you received as part of the investigative bundle?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: There were no modifications made to this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that we know what we're talking about, what does this map represent? What is the purpose of this map?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: It is a map of the municipality of Suva Reka, showing all of the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, we get the fine detail of little hamlets, et cetera, et cetera, that might be referred to by witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Clerk.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 4, map 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still staying with that municipality, in tab 12 of the binder that we had hoped to provide to the Court, but it was K46, is a town map of Suva Reka. Do you have that? Here it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's on the ELMO. Now, there are two -- this is a town map of Suva Reka, and did you -- this is prepared by computers in the office of the ICTY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, sir, what is depicted in this map?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Apart from the municipal area of the town of Suva Reka, there are two additional points marked. Point 1 is marked as the Berisha household. Point number 2 is marked as a cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And those red lines, sir, those, I take it, are major roads, are they, the red lines from starting at the top of the photograph working down to the bottom and then the one that sort of forms a triangle near points 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct. That is the main road between Prizren and Stimlje, and this is a main road which takes you to -- I think it's Studencani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the very bottom of that map, we see that the road leads to -- there's a town called Prizren located at the bottom; is that correct? That's the road to Prizren?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct. I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I think it's already been marked as Exhibit 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on, if I may, then, sir, to the Pec municipality, or Peje, map 6 of Exhibit 3, please. Do you have that on the -- okay. That's on the ELMO. Can you again, sir, very briefly describe what this represents.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: It represents the routes taken by displaced persons from the city of Pec through Decani, Djakovica, Prizren, to the border of Qafe e Morina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's near the bottom of the map.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There also appear to be arrows leading upwards from Peje, or Pec, toward Montenegro. What is that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: The arrow on the bottom shows a route from Pec to Rozaje on the main road. The second arrow shows an alternate route through the mountains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That was -- formerly K7 is now map 6 of Exhibit 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part of K8, sir, you have a -- and that is for the Pec municipality, or Peje municipality. Just so that we're clear, Pec and Peje, those are just -- one is a Serbian way of expressing the name of the municipality, and Peje is the Albanian way of expressing the municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So although on the map it says "Peje" and on your map it says "Pec," we're talking about the same municipality?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, this was one of those maps that was provided, showing all the little villages in the Peje or Pec municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The exhibit now on the ELMO. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is where I lose -- this is part of Exhibit 4, I believe it is, Madam --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 4, map 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And might I also ask you to look at Exhibit K55, or what we called K55, about to become an exhibit. That would be at tab 13 of the material that was provided.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Witness, very briefly: I take it this is pretty self-explanatory. It's a town map of Pec, or Peje. Are the red lines -- perhaps you could tell us: The red lines, are those roadways?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That's correct. The red lines are the major roads --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about --

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: -- through the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the little cross-stitches, the black little hash marks? What are those?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: Those marks there are the railway line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And at bottom of this map - and I'm looking at it in a rectangle -- a horizontal, rectangle form - it says, "to Decani and Djakovica." That's the road to Decani and Djakovica; and to the north -- I'm sorry. To the top of the map, it's to Mitrovica; is that correct? Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 702 to 713.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to the left, as I'm looking at the map, to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to the right, to Klina and Pristina.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were there any other markings that you placed on this map that you want to point to the Court's attention?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: No, there are not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, if we may, then. I'm now going to turn, if I may, to map 7, which is the Kosovska Mitrovica site. And first of all, part of K7 is now map 7. That's on the ELMO. Again, very briefly, sir, what does this tell us?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: It depicts the routes taken by displaced persons from the city of Kosovska Mitrovica, through Klina, Djakovica, Peje, Istok, to border crossings at Qafe e Morina and at Rozaje with Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, sir, just so that I'm clear, the yellow markings on this map show us two major border exit points; is that correct? Is that what this shows, or am I wrong in interpreting this?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: No. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One with the border of Albania, at the bottom of the map, and one at the border of Montenegro, near the top of the map; is that it?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the yellow lines are the various routes that people took to get there?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many of them going through Prizren in order to get to Albania?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN SPARGO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That was map 7, part of Exhibit 3, Madam Clerk? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
